In this chapter and the next, we'll cover the techniques of correlation and regression. Whereas the $z$, $t$, and ANOVA statistics we've covered so far deal with examining differences between groups, correlation and regression focus on associations between variables. As we'll see, though, this isn't as big a difference as you might expect. Correlation and regression are just another extension of the basic ideas of variability, sampling, and probability that have powered all of our inferential statistics so far.

## From groups to pairs

In Chapter 12, we imagined giving people $10 and telling them to spend it either on themselves or on someone else. I based that idea on a real experiment, in which people randomly assigned to spend a small amount of cash on someone else reported being happier later that day than people assigned to spend it on themselves [@dunn2008spending]. At the end of the chapter I made a big to-do about how one study is never the final word on anything.

What I didn't mention is that the researchers actually did more than one kind of study. In the same paper, they reported another in which they didn't give out cash or assign anyone to anything. Instead they just surveyed a representative sample of 632 Americans, asking how happy they were in general and how much they spent in a typical month on gifts for other people and donations to charity.

How might we analyze the data to see whether spending on others goes with being happier? In recetn chapters we've compared groups with the $t$ or $F$ statistic. But we don't really have groups in this case, just two answers from each person. I suppose we could *make* some groups. Maybe a lot of people tell us they spent nothing on others that month. So we could split the sample into people who spent something and people who spent nothing, and compare the two groups' mean happiness with an independent-samples $t$ test. Even though group membership isn't randomly assigned, the $t$ test can still tell us whether the difference in means is more than we'd expect by chance.

But that would throw away a lot of good information. Everyone who spent anything gets lumped together, so we lose any distinction between someone who spent $5 on others and someone who spent $500. There has to be a better way! How might we make use of each person's actual amount spent?

::: {#quiz-correlation-pairs}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-pairs.qmd >}}
:::

The idea @quiz-correlation-pairs was getting at is to look at the relationship between two variables by examining how they vary together. The question isn't whether two sets of scores *differ*, on average, but whether the two go *together*: do people who spend more on others tend to be happier?

Like our other analyses, we still make use of averages and deviations. The new idea is that we're looking at the consistency of two different sets of deviations. When a score on one variable is above its mean, is there a consistent pattern in the other variable? If the correlation is positive, the other variable will also tend to be above its mean: someone who spends more than average on others would tend to be happier than average. Correspondingly, someone who spends below average would tend to be less happy than average. On the other hand, if the correlation were negative---more prosocial spending was associated with lower happiness---we would find that a high spender would tend to be less happy than average. This is the essence of correlation; it's all about the consistency of pairs of deviations.

Here's what that idea looks like with some data. (These aren't the real survey responses, just a handful of made-up people to illustrate.)

::::: {#act-same-side .callout-tip .interactive}

Counting dots in the four sections like this is a rough version of what a correlation does. The real math also takes into account precisely how far each person is from the two means, so that someone far above average on both counts for more than someone only just above. And just as with a difference between group means, we'll need to know whether an apparent pattern is more than we'd expect by chance.

### What would it mean?

Now I know you're excited to do the math, and we'll get to it soon. But first, let's distinguish two closely related terms. The **correlation statistic**, also called a **correlation coefficient**, is the number that quantifies the relationship between two variables. That's what we'll get to calculating in the next section. But **correlational** describes the research design. Before we calculate the statistic, let's think about how this kind of design changes what conclusions we can draw from our data, and what kind of follow-up analyses might be useful.

Remember, we have two different designs testing the same general idea---that prosocial spending goes with happiness. One tests the idea by comparing randomly assigned groups, the other by looking for a correlation in survey responses. Suppose both studies found what the researchers expected. People assigned to spend money on others were happier, and people who said they spent more on others were happier. Do those two findings mean the same thing?

::: {#quiz-correlation-designs}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-designs.qmd >}}
:::

The actual survey, using the appropriate analysis[^dunn-regression], found that people who spent more on others did tend to be happier. The association was small, but statistically significant. But does that mean that spending on others makes people happier? Not necessarily. For one thing, maybe people who earn more money are happier, and they tend to give more to charity and stuff. The relationship between charitable spending and happiness could just be a byproduct of that other relationship.

In fact, the researchers anticipated this possibility. They asked people about their income, and taking it into account barely changed the association between spending on others and happiness. So in this case, income doesn't explain away the relationship.

[^dunn-regression]: They actually used regression to do this, which is the topic of the next chapter. But it's closely related to correlation, so it still makes for a valid illustration of the point here.

But that only rules out one alternative. I'm sure you can imagine others. The researchers hadn't measured everything that might make people both more generous and happier. There's also the issue of reverse causality: maybe being happier makes people more generous, rather than the other way around. As Dunn and colleagues put it themselves, "the correlational nature of this design precludes causal inferences."

That's why they did the experiment, giving people some money and telling them who to spend it on. But that kind of research has its own limitations. In order to establish causality, it creates a fairly unusual situation. In everyday life, people aren't usually handed an envelope of cash and told how to spend it. So the experiment gives a clear answer to a narrow, somewhat contrived question. The survey answers a more realistic question, less conclusively. Together they contribute to a body of evidence, but neither is definitive on its own.

## The correlation coefficient

Now we can get into the details of the correlation statistic itself. The statistic we'll use is called **Pearson's $r$ correlation coefficient**, named after Karl Pearson---the statistician Gosset went to study with in Chapter 11. But its development also involved another familiar figure: Francis Galton, whose board of bouncing balls helped us think about sampling in Chapter 7.

Galton was interested in how people's physical characteristics varied together. Taller people tend to have bigger feet, for example, but the association isn't perfect. How could you put a number on how consistently the two measurements go together? One useful step was to express each measurement relative to its own variability. Being one inch above the average height would be less surprising than having feet that are one inch longer than average. We've already encountered the same basic idea with $z$-scores: putting different measurements on a comparable scale [@galton1888corelations].

Pearson developed the mathematical treatment behind the coefficient we use today [@pearson1896regression]. Galton had already used the letter $r$ in his work on regression, the closely related technique we'll meet in the next chapter. So correlation and regression have been intertwined from the beginning.

### Characteristics

The correlation coefficient is a single number that quantifies the **strength** and **direction** of a linear association between two quantitative variables.[^other-correlations] Because of how it's calculated, $r$ can range from $-1$ to $1$.

[^other-correlations]: The same calculation turns up under a few other names. Pearson's $r$ calculated on ranks is *Spearman's rank correlation*. If one variable is quantitative and the other is coded 0 or 1, it's a *point-biserial correlation*. Coding the two spending groups in Chapter 12 that way gives $r = .28$ (with spend-on-other coded 1), and testing it gives the same $t(8) = 0.82$ we got by comparing means. If both variables are coded 0 or 1, the correlation is called *phi*.

The absolute value quantifies the strength of the relationship, or, in other words, the consistency of the association between the variables. The stronger and more consistent their association, the closer the correlation will be to 1 (or $-1$). The weaker and less consistent their relationship, the closer the correlation will be to 0.

The sign, positive or negative, indicates the direction of the correlation. A positive correlation is one for which increases in one variable are associated with increases in the other---or, correspondingly, lower scores on one are associated with lower scores on the other. A negative correlation means that higher scores on one variable are associated with lower scores on the other---that they move in opposite directions.

These characteristics are illustrated in the scatterplots in @fig-cor-characteristics.

:::: {#fig-cor-characteristics}
::: {.sfs-figure-row}

:::
Scatterplots illustrating various correlation coefficients. I've drawn an ellipse to summarize the shape of the cloud. The stronger the correlation, the closer the cloud comes to forming a straight line.
::::

At zero, the ellipse in @fig-cor-characteristics is basically a circle, with no upward or downward tendency, meaning that there is no consistent linear relationship between the two variables. As the correlation gets stronger, the ellipse gets longer and thinner. A "perfect correlation" of either $1$ or $-1$ means that every change in one variable is accompanied by a proportional change in the other; the dots fall into a straight line, and the ellipse becomes a line. In a sense, the correlation coefficient is a measure of how closely the data points follow a straight-line pattern.[^scatterplot-scale-note]

[^scatterplot-scale-note]: One thing to be careful about with this picture. I've put the two variables on matching scales, so one standard deviation takes up the same distance on either axis. Stretch one axis and even the uncorrelated cloud could look long and thin. Measuring height in centimeters instead of inches, for example, doesn't change the correlation, even if it changes the appearance of the plot. What matters is how consistently the two variables go together, relative to their separate variability, rather than how steep or stretched the pattern looks on the page.

## Calculating $r$

Now let's see how to calculate Pearson's $r$. It's based on the ideas of **variability** and **covariability**.

You're very familiar with variability by now. It's the quantification of how much each variable varies, how widely spread or closely clustered scores are. Covariability is the new idea here. It quantifies how much $X$ and $Y$ vary together: to what extent are changes in $X$ associated with corresponding changes in $Y$? When $X$ is above its mean, does $Y$ tend to be above its mean too (or below it)? Put another way, if there were no covariability at all, variation in $Y$ would be completely unrelated to the variation in $X$.

Here's the equation for Pearson's $r$:

$$ r = \frac{SP}{\sqrt{SS_X SS_Y}} $$ {#eq-pearson-r}

$SS_X$ and $SS_Y$ should look familiar. $SS$, as usual, refers to the sum of squared deviations. So here we have the separate sums of squares for variable $X$ and variable $Y$ to quantify their separate variability in the denominator. And we have this new quantity, $SP$, which quantifies the covariability of $X$ and $Y$.

I'll explain in a moment exactly what $SP$ is. But first, let me point out that if every change in $X$ had a proportional change in $Y$, then the covariability in the numerator would be as big in magnitude as their separate variabilities, combined in the denominator. The correlation would equal one or negative one. In other words, all the variability is covariability. Every point falls on a straight line, just as we saw when the ellipse collapsed. There is no variability that isn't shared. So the more unshared variability there is, the closer the correlation coefficient will be to zero, When there is no shared linear variability at all, the numerator will be zero, and so will the correlation coefficient. This is why $r$ can only vary between negative one and positive one.

### $SS$ and $SP$

Before getting to $SP$, let's recap sum of squares. To calculate the sum of squared deviations, we square the deviation scores. And another way of saying that we square something is to say we multiply it by itself. So here are two equivalent ways of writing the equation for sum of squares:

$$ SS = \Sigma(X - M)^2 $$

$$ SS = \Sigma(X - M)(X - M) $$

The reason I point this out is that $SP$ does something quite similar, but instead of multiplying deviations by *themselves*, we multiply them by *one another*. Our numerator, $SP$, is the sum of products. Products refer to the product of the deviations. We multiply the deviations for variable $X$ by the deviations for variable $Y$ to get their products. Then we sum those products to get the sum of products.

$$ SP = \Sigma(X - M_X)(Y - M_Y) $$

I hope that by juxtaposing this with the sum of squares formula, you can see the conceptual link. The sum of squares quantifies the variability of an individual variable by multiplying its deviations by themselves. The sum of products quantifies the covariability of two variables by multiplying their deviations by one another.[^sp-computational]

[^sp-computational]: As with the sum of squares back in Chapter 4, there's also a computational formula for the sum of products, and it's similarly related: $SP = \Sigma XY - \frac{(\Sigma X)(\Sigma Y)}{n}$. Again, this is equivalent to the definitional formula. We'll stick with the definitional approach.

### Worked example

Let's work through a simple example to see how the sum of products is calculated. Suppose we're interested in how the number of cups of coffee a student drinks is related to their test score. Maybe the caffeine will increase alertness and cognitive performance, leading to better test scores. We have data for seven students, as shown in @tbl-coffee-scores.

| Participant | Coffee (cups), $X$ | Test score, $Y$ |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 90 |
| B | 0.5 | 60 |
| C | 0.5 | 85 |
| D | 1 | 65 |
| E | 1.5 | 50 |
| F | 1.5 | 65 |
| G | 2 | 75 |

: Cups of coffee and test scores for seven students. {#tbl-coffee-scores}

Before we work through the full calculation, let's picture the two sums of squares and the sum of products for this little dataset.

::::: {#act-sum-of-products .callout-tip .interactive .with-controls}

:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Means" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":false,"square-mode":"residual","show-ss":false,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":false,"show-products":false,"show-sp":false,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
First we need the two means. The dashed lines mark the mean cups of coffee, $M_X = 1$, and the mean test score, $M_Y = 70$. Between them they split the plot into four quarters.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="$SS_X$" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":true,"square-mode":"x","show-ss":true,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":true,"show-products":false,"show-sp":false,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
Start with coffee consumption. Each horizontal deviation from $M_X = 1$ becomes the side of a square. Add the seven squared deviations: $SS_X = 1 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 1 = 3$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="$SS_Y$" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":true,"square-mode":"y","show-ss":true,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":true,"show-products":false,"show-sp":false,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
Now do the same for test scores. Each vertical deviation from $M_Y = 70$ becomes the side of a square. Add the seven squared deviations: $SS_Y = 400 + 100 + 225 + 25 + 400 + 25 + 25 = 1200$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Deviations" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":false,"square-mode":"residual","show-ss":false,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":true,"show-products":false,"show-sp":false,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
Each student has two deviations: how far they are from the mean on $X$, and how far they are from the mean on $Y$. Student A drank 1 cup less than average and scored 20 points above average. Student G is above average on both.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Products" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":false,"square-mode":"residual","show-ss":false,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":true,"show-products":true,"show-sp":false,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
Now we multiply each student's two deviations. On the plot, that product is a rectangle: one deviation wide and the other deviation tall. Students A, C, E, and F are above one mean and below the other, so their deviations have opposite signs and their products are negative. Those are the orange rectangles with dashed outlines. Students B and G are on the same side of both means, so their products are positive. Student D is exactly at the mean for coffee, so their product is zero.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="$SP$" data-action='{"points":[[0,90,"A"],[0.5,60,"B"],[0.5,85,"C"],[1,65,"D"],[1.5,50,"E"],[1.5,65,"F"],[2,75,"G"]],"x-domain":[-0.25,2.5],"y-domain":[40,100],"point-labels":true,"product-labels":true,"show-squares":false,"square-mode":"residual","show-ss":false,"show-means":true,"show-deviations":true,"show-products":true,"show-sp":true,"show-r":false,"draggable":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
Add up the products and we have the sum of products: $SP = -20 + 5 - 7.5 + 0 - 10 - 2.5 + 5 = -30$. The negative products outweigh the positive ones, so $SP$ comes out negative.
:::
::::

:::::

To calculate those pieces by hand, it's easiest to make a table, much like the ones we've put together as part of calculating standard deviation. List the scores in one column, compute the mean, then add a column for the deviation of each score from the mean, then a column for the squared deviations, then sum the squared deviations in that column to get $SS$. It's the same deal here, but we do it for both variables, $X$ (cups of coffee) and $Y$ (test scores).

Following that process gets us both $SS_X$ and $SS_Y$, the values for the denominator of the $r$ equation. The last step is $SP$. That goes in one more column. To fill in its values, we just multiply the deviations we already computed for $X$ and $Y$ to get the products. (To be clear, we're multiplying the deviations, not squared deviations.) Then we sum those products to get the sum of products, which here is $-30$.

| $X$ | $X - M_X$ | $(X - M_X)^2$ | $Y$ | $Y - M_Y$ | $(Y - M_Y)^2$ | $(X - M_X)(Y - M_Y)$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | $-1$ | 1 | 90 | 20 | 400 | $-20$ |
| 0.5 | $-0.5$ | 0.25 | 60 | $-10$ | 100 | 5 |
| 0.5 | $-0.5$ | 0.25 | 85 | 15 | 225 | $-7.5$ |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 65 | $-5$ | 25 | 0 |
| 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 50 | $-20$ | 400 | $-10$ |
| 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 65 | $-5$ | 25 | $-2.5$ |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 75 | 5 | 25 | 5 |
| | | $SS_X = 3$ | | | $SS_Y = 1200$ | $SP = -30$ |

: Deviations, squared deviations, and products for the coffee data. $M_X = 1$; $M_Y = 70$. {#tbl-r-definitional}

That gives us everything we need to calculate the correlation coefficient:

$$r = \frac{SP}{\sqrt{SS_X SS_Y}} = \frac{-30}{\sqrt{3 \times 1200}} = \frac{-30}{60} = -.50$$

::: {#quiz-correlation-calculate-r}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-calculate-r.qmd >}}
:::

## A correlation test, step by step

So we've calculated a correlation coefficient, $r$, for our little coffee consumption and test performance data set. The correlation came out negative: drinking more coffee was associated with lower test scores. But is that a significant relationship, or just due to chance? To know that, we need to submit the data to a full hypothesis test, following the same basic procedure we've used for every other hypothesis test.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

As always, we begin by formally stating our hypotheses. And as with every other hypothesis test we've done, we're going to use samples of scores, but we don't actually care about those samples. We're interested in the population or populations that produce them. So our hypotheses concern the relationship that exists or doesn't exist in the population.

The lowercase letter $r$ is the correlation coefficient we calculate for our sample; we use the Greek letter $\rho$ to represent the population parameter, the correlation within the population. The null hypothesis says that there's no relationship in the population, so $\rho$ is zero. We'll use a nondirectional alternative, which says that it isn't:

$$ H_0: \rho = 0 $$

$$ H_1: \rho \ne 0 $$

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

We calculated the correlation coefficient, $r$, for our sample already, but we don't actually *test* that statistic. Pearson's $r$ is a measure of effect size. It quantifies the magnitude of association between two variables according to our data. It doesn't allow for a probabilistic decision about whether the association is likely to exist in the population. At least, not directly.

This is going to sound weird, but the test statistic for a correlation is actually a $t$ statistic. We'll see how to calculate that $t$ statistic in Step 3.

For now, we just need to know its degrees of freedom so we can determine the critical $t$ values. And for bivariate correlations, degrees of freedom are $n$, the number of pairs of scores, minus two. Each student contributes one pair---their coffee consumption and their test score---so our seven students give us seven observations of the relationship, even though we've recorded fourteen scores.

But why subtract two? Here's where the connection with regression helps. We can summarize a cloud of points by fitting a straight line through it, called a **regression line**. We'll work out how to fit it and use it for predictions in the next chapter. For now, think about what would happen with just two points, with different scores on both variables. We could always draw a straight line passing through both, fitting perfectly. The correlation would be one or negative one. There'd be no opportunity for either point to deviate from the line, because those two points determine the line itself. It's only when we add more observations that we can see any scatter around it. So fitting the line uses up two degrees of freedom, leaving $n - 2$ deviations free to vary.

As before, we can check the $t$ table to find the critical values. Since our little example dataset has seven pairs of scores, our degrees of freedom are seven minus two, which is five. We'll use $\alpha = .05$. Looking in the two-tailed .05 column gives critical values of $\pm 2.571$. We reject the null if $t < -2.571$ or $t > 2.571$.

::: {#tbl-correlation-critical}
{{< interactive-figure correlationCriticalTable makeTTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the coffee test","df":{"from":1,"to":7},"alphas":[0.1,0.05,0.025,0.01,0.005],"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","confidence":false,"interactive":false,"selected":{"df":5,"tail":"two","alpha":0.05}}' fallback="t table excerpt for 1 through 7 degrees of freedom, highlighting the two-tailed .05 critical value of 2.571 at df = 5." >}}

An excerpt of the $t$ table, with the $df = 5$ row highlighted. The two-tailed $.05$ heading puts $.025$ in each tail.
:::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

We already found $r = -.50$ (@tbl-r-definitional). But like I said, we don't test the $r$ statistic itself. Rather, we need to convert the $r$ value into a kind of $t$ statistic to see how improbable it is, given the variability in the data, that we would have observed an association this strong or stronger if no association actually exists in the population, as our null hypothesis assumes.

First, recall the general conceptual form of any $t$ statistic (@eq-t-structure). It's composed of a sample statistic minus a population parameter in the numerator and a standard error in the denominator, to reveal how much your observed sample statistic deviates from the null expected value in relation to the standard error---the amount you'd expect the sample to deviate from the population value due to sampling error.

Here, the specific form that takes is:

$$ t = \frac{r - \rho}{s_r} $$ {#eq-correlation-t}

Here $r$ is the correlation coefficient, $\rho$ is the population correlation assumed by the null hypothesis (zero), and $s_r$ is the standard error of the correlation. That standard error is found like this:

$$ s_r = \sqrt{\frac{1 - r^2}{n - 2}} $$ {#eq-correlation-se}

There's a new ingredient here: $r^2$, the correlation squared. Remember how $\eta^2$ in Chapter 14 told us what proportion of the total variability was accounted for by differences between the groups? $r^2$ does a similar job for a linear relationship: it tells us the proportion of the variability in one variable that's shared with the other. For our coffee data, $r^2 = (-.50)^2 = .25$. So 25% of the variability in test scores is shared with coffee consumption, leaving 75% unaccounted for by that relationship. In terms of the scatterplot, that's the variability in the points above and below the regression line. That's the $1 - r^2$ in the numerator.

So the standard error reflects the variability left over after accounting for the relationship, divided by the degrees of freedom, with a square root to undo the squaring. A stronger correlation means less scatter around the line relative to the total variability in $Y$, making this standard error smaller. And for the same correlation, more pairs of scores make it smaller too. Both should make sense: a clearer pattern and more observations give us a more precise estimate.

For our coffee data, that works out like this:

$$t = \frac{r - \rho}{s_r} = \frac{-.50 - 0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{1 - (-.50)^2}{7 - 2}}} = \frac{-.50}{.387} = -1.29$$

### Step 4: Make a decision

Our $t = -1.29$ falls short of the critical value of $\pm 2.571$ for five degrees of freedom, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis despite the seemingly strong correlation.

::: {#fig-correlation-decision}
{{< interactive-figure correlationTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"t","df":5,"title":"Null distribution: df = 5","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[-5,5],"xTicks":5,"labels":{"x":"t statistic"},"shade":{"tail":"two","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":-2.570582,"label":"−2.571","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":2.570582,"label":"+2.571","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":-1.290994,"label":"t = −1.29","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null t distribution with 5 degrees of freedom. The two rejection regions lie beyond ±2.571; the observed t of −1.29 falls between them." >}}

The observed $t = -1.29$ falls between the critical values of the null $t$ distribution with $df = 5$.
:::

The corresponding two-tailed $p$-value is approximately $.25$, well above our $\alpha$ of $.05$.

## Reporting and interpreting the results

### Reporting results

As always, we need to report the results of our hypothesis test. Here, that statement will include the value of the correlation coefficient, Pearson's $r$, its degrees of freedom, and the $p$-value for the correlation.

> Drinking more coffee was associated with lower test scores, but the correlation did not reach statistical significance; $r(5) = -.50$, $p = .25$.

### Interpreting the results

So what do we make of our result? We failed to reject the null hypothesis, but that doesn't establish that there's no relationship. We only have seven pairs of scores. Our $r = -.50$ describes a fairly strong negative association in this sample; the hypothesis test tells us that, with so few observations, it isn't enough evidence to reject the null.

::: {#quiz-correlation-significance}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-significance.qmd >}}
:::

As for how to interpret Pearson's $r$ as a measure of effect size, you might remember from Chapter 9 that Cohen offered some rules of thumb for interpreting Cohen's $d$. Well, he offered some for Pearson's $r$ as well. Cohen suggested that a correlation of .1 should be considered small, .3 medium, and .5 large. However, like I mentioned before, these are just rules of thumb, and Cohen himself strongly cautioned against over-reliance on them.

We've already met Funder and Ozer's [-@funder2019evaluating] argument that small effects can matter, back in Chapter 9. Their paper offers some alternative benchmarks based on the kinds of effects found in psychological research and the consequences those effects can have. Let's get a feel for what they mean.

| $r$ | Cohen | Funder and Ozer |
|:--:|:--|:--|
| .05 | | Very small |
| .10 | Small | Small |
| .20 | | Medium |
| .30 | Medium | Large |
| .40 | | Very large |
| .50 | Large | |

: Rough benchmarks for interpreting $r$ as an effect size. {#tbl-r-benchmarks}

These are invented point clouds of 100 observations each. As you step through, the same points move to produce each correlation, with the axes kept on the same scale. We're showing positive correlations, but the same descriptions of strength apply to negative ones.

::::: {#act-correlation-effect-sizes .callout-tip .interactive}
## How small is a small correlation?

{{< interactive-figure correlationEffectSizes makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.05,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4},"controlSet":"correlation","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"ticks":"none","axisLabels":false,"xDomain":[0,100],"yDomain":[0,100],"pointRadius":4,"maxWidth":"28rem"}' fallback="A five-step tutorial showing invented correlations of .05, .10, .20, .30, and .40 on fixed axes, with an ellipse summarizing the point cloud. The upward pattern becomes clearer, but substantial scatter remains even at .40." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Very small: .05" data-action='{"generate":{"r":0.05,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4},"animate":false}'}
At $r = .05$, there's barely any visible pattern. Knowing someone's $X$ score would tell us very little about their $Y$ score. Funder and Ozer call this *very small* for understanding a single event. But if a small influence operates repeatedly, its consequences can add up. Small doesn't necessarily mean unimportant.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Small: .10" data-action='{"generate":{"r":0.1,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4}}'}
At $r = .10$, the pattern is still faint. Funder and Ozer call this *small*: a weak clue about any one outcome, but potentially consequential across many occasions or many people. Notice how much the points overlap. A small correlation leaves plenty of room for people to differ from the general tendency.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Medium: .20" data-action='{"generate":{"r":0.2,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4}}'}
At $r = .20$, the upward pattern is getting clearer, though the cloud is still broad and the ellipse is a long way from collapsing to a line. Funder and Ozer call this *medium*, with some practical use even for individual outcomes. It won't tell us exactly what someone will score, but it can give us a useful improvement on guessing without that information.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Large: .30" data-action='{"generate":{"r":0.3,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4}}'}
At $r = .30$, Funder and Ozer call the effect *large*, with potentially substantial consequences over both short and long periods. That might sound surprising if you were expecting a long, thin ellipse. But large in psychological research doesn't mean close to perfect. There's still a lot going on besides this one relationship.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Very large: .40" data-action='{"generate":{"r":0.4,"n":100,"seed":31,"round":4}}'}
At $r = .40$, the pattern is clearer again. Funder and Ozer call this *very large* for psychological research, and urge particular scrutiny: unusually large estimates can shrink in bigger samples or replications. That doesn't mean a correlation this large must be wrong. It means we should look carefully at how reliably it has been estimated.
:::
::::

:::::

To make the accumulation idea more concrete, imagine a study habit that gives you a small advantage on any one quiz. It wouldn't guarantee a good score; the questions you happen to get and plenty of other things would matter too. But if the habit keeps helping across a whole course of quizzes, those small advantages could add up to a meaningful difference in what you learn and the grade you earn. The consequences accumulate; we're not saying that the correlation itself automatically gets bigger over time.

So from this you can see how context-dependent our interpretation of effect size should be. These descriptions are starting points for thinking about a result, not boundaries that tell us whether it matters. What are we measuring, how reliable is the estimate, and what would a relationship of this size mean in practice?

Suppose our seven students were the first seven in a study of 300. (The rest are invented too.) Across all 300, the correlation between coffee and test score is only $-.15$. With just seven students, a few scores can make quite a difference to $r$, and in this case the first seven made the relationship look much stronger. Yet it's the smaller correlation that reaches statistical significance, $t(298) = -2.62$, $p = .009$. With that many students, a correlation this far from zero or farther would be unusual if the population correlation were zero.

### Correlation and causation

As we saw at the beginning of this chapter with the prosocial spending survey, correlational research has its limits. Knowing that charitable spending is associated with happiness doesn't tell us whether spending causes happiness, or whether happier people are more likely to spend on others, or whether some other factor is behind both. In that research, the authors also measured income, and found that it was associated with both spending and happiness. But even after accounting for income, the association between spending and happiness remained. How did they do that?

Let's apply the same logic to our coffee and test score example. We found a negative correlation between coffee consumption and test scores, but we don't know whether drinking coffee is causing lower test scores, or whether students who expect to do poorly on the exam are drinking more coffee, or whether some other factor is behind both. Maybe students who haven't been sleeping are both drinking more coffee and scoring lower on the exam.

So suppose the study also recorded each student's average nightly sleep over the week before the exam. (That sleep came before the morning's coffee, so the coffee can't have caused it.) Here are our seven students again, with their sleep.

| Participant | Coffee (cups) | Test score | Sleep (hours) |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 90 | 9 |
| B | 0.5 | 60 | 8 |
| C | 0.5 | 85 | 8 |
| D | 1 | 65 | 5 |
| E | 1.5 | 50 | 6 |
| F | 1.5 | 65 | 6 |
| G | 2 | 75 | 7 |

: The seven students from @tbl-coffee-scores, now with their average nightly sleep over the week before the exam. {#tbl-coffee-sleep-scores}

With three variables we can calculate three correlations, one for each pair. @tbl-coffee-sleep-correlations shows them for all 300 students in what's called a **correlation matrix**. Pick a row and a column and read across and down to where they meet. We've only filled in the lower half because correlating sleep with coffee gives us exactly the same number as correlating coffee with sleep.

| | Coffee | Test score | Sleep |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Coffee | --- | | |
| Test score | $-.15$ | --- | |
| Sleep | $-.35$ | $.30$ | --- |

: Correlation matrix for coffee, test score, and sleep across all 300 students in the invented study. {#tbl-coffee-sleep-correlations}

Students who slept less tended to drink more coffee ($r = -.35$) and get lower test scores ($r = .30$). So how much of the relationship between coffee and test score is still there once we take sleep into account?

We can work that out with a **partial correlation**. Think of two students who got the same amount of sleep. Would knowing which one drank more coffee still tell us anything about who scored higher? For each student, we work out how much more or less coffee they drank than we'd predict from their sleep using a straight line. Then we do the same for their test score. The partial correlation is the correlation between those two sets of deviations. We can calculate it directly from the three correlations in the table. Here $X$ is coffee, $Y$ is test score, and $Z$ is sleep.

$$ r_{XY \cdot Z} = \frac{r_{XY} - r_{XZ}\,r_{YZ}}{\sqrt{(1 - r_{XZ}^2)(1 - r_{YZ}^2)}} $$ {#eq-partial-r}

$$ r_{XY \cdot Z} = \frac{-.15 - (-.35)(.30)}{\sqrt{(1 - (-.35)^2)(1 - .30^2)}} = \frac{-.045}{.894} = -.05 $$

::: {#fig-coffee-test-third-variable}

{{< include resources/figures/coffee-test-third-variable.svg >}}

Accounting for sleep. The solid lines show sleep's correlations with coffee and with test score. The dashed line shows the correlation between coffee and test score that remains after accounting for sleep: $-.05$, down from $-.15$. All values are invented.

:::

Accounting for sleep brings the correlation much closer to zero, from $-.15$ to $-.05$. Compare that with the spending survey at the beginning of the chapter. There, taking income into account barely changed the association between spending on others and happiness.

::: {#quiz-correlation-partial}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-partial.qmd >}}
:::

For the full sample of 300, the partial correlation falls short of statistical significance, $t(297) = -0.87$, $p = .39$. But we can see how much the association shrank by comparing the two coefficients themselves. Crossing the $.05$ threshold doesn't tell us how much anything changed.

Does that settle what caused the lower scores? Even if these were real students, we'd only have accounted for the sleep we measured. Other differences between students could still be involved. That's the advantage of random assignment back in Chapter 12. It gives even the differences we didn't think to measure the same distribution across groups on average. What lets us draw a causal conclusion is how the study was done. Running a $t$ test on groups the students chose for themselves wouldn't turn our survey into an experiment.

::: {#quiz-correlation-causation}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-your-turn-causation.qmd >}}
:::

### Correlation assumptions

#### Independence

Remember the related-samples $t$ test in Chapter 13? Each child raced twice. We worked out a difference for each child, and those differences had to be independent from one child to the next. Here each student gives us a pair of scores. We're interested in how the two scores *within* a pair go together. Independence applies *between* pairs.

Suppose our seven rows came from one student who sat seven exams. We'd still have seven dots on the scatterplot, but we'd only have one student. Treating those dots as seven independent students would give us the wrong basis for our $p$-value. To judge independence we need to know where the rows came from.

#### Linearity

When I defined Pearson's $r$, I said it measures a *linear* association: how consistently the points follow a straight line. So if we calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient, we're assuming our variables are related linearly.

But variables can also be related in ways that a straight line doesn't capture. As $X$ increases, $Y$ might decrease at first, then start increasing. There's a real, predictable relationship, but it changes direction along the way. Pearson's $r$ can't capture that.

:::: {#fig-scatter-nonlinear}

The linear correlation is r = 0 despite the clear pattern." >}}
:::
Three examples of nonlinear relationships: a U-shaped relationship, a wave, and something entirely contrived---data arranged in the shape of a star. None are random or unpredictable, but all three have exactly the same linear correlation: $r = 0$, because it only captures linear relationships.
::::

So a correlation of zero doesn't necessarily mean that there's no relationship. The points in the first two plots follow curves, and the last lot are arranged in a star. None of those patterns is captured by a straight line. This is why it's worth looking at the scatterplot before trying to summarize the relationship with a single number.
